analysis.one_liner: Gives Supreme Court justices 18-year terms, with a new seat opening every two years.
analysis.headline: Supreme Court term limits were proposed with 86 Democratic cosponsors in May 2025 and were referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on them since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set fixed 18-year terms for Supreme Court justices instead of lifetime tenure. The president would nominate one justice every two years, in the first and third years after each presidential election, and the Senate would have 90 days to vote. The nine sitting justices would keep their seats for now but would be retired in order of seniority as new justices are sworn in. If a seat sits empty, a retired justice would be chosen by a publicly visible random process to fill in temporarily.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who wants a Supreme Court that turns over on a predictable schedule rather than depending on when a justice happens to die, retire, or be accused of misconduct. A regular two-year rotation would mean every president gets the same number of appointments, every voter knows the stakes before an election, and no justice holds power for 40 years. People who want the Court's rulings to reflect the country they are deciding cases for, rather than the views of a small group selected decades earlier, benefit the most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting a regularly refreshed Court

how_it_helps.text: Replaces lifetime tenure with a single 18-year term for each justice, so no single justice can shape the law for four decades or more.

Sets a fixed schedule of one new justice every two years in the first and third years after presidential elections, ending the random vacancy lottery in which one president may fill two seats and another none.
Requires the Senate to vote on each Supreme Court nominee within 90 days (120 for a second nomination), making it harder for the Senate to leave a seat open indefinitely.
Phases out lifetime tenure for current justices fairly, retiring them one at a time in order of longest service as new justices arrive, so no justice is singled out.

analysis.who_pays: The nine current justices, who would lose the lifetime seats they hold under the Constitution's default 'good behavior' tenure, and the political leaders of both parties who currently benefit from the Court's exact composition and from the power to reshape it with a lucky vacancy. No ordinary person pays a dollar.

drawbacks.text: The bill would retire sitting justices by operation of law as new justices are commissioned; critics argue the Constitution gives federal judges their offices during 'good behavior' and that cutting a sitting justice's tenure short invites a court challenge the bill may not survive.

When a seat is empty, the bill lets the Chief Justice pick any retired justice through a 'randomized' process to sit temporarily, which is a novel, untested mechanism that could produce unusual temporary benches and unpredictable rulings.

The fixed schedule means a justice must be nominated every two years regardless of need or candidate quality, which could force rushed or slot-filling appointments in years when neither party is eager to make one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — fixed terms instead of lifetime tenure — is used by most modern democracies and would make the Court's composition a predictable result of elections rather than of death and retirement timing. The honest weakness is the bill's treatment of current justices: forcing sitting justices into retirement is the provision most likely to fail a constitutional test, and a court might uphold term limits only for future justices, delaying any change by decades. The temporary-recall mechanism for empty seats is also untested and awkward. A version applying only to future justices would be legally safer but slower to matter.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has not held a hearing or scheduled any action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the bill on May 21, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
86 of the 217 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican did.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote after the referral, leaving the bill pending in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet, because the bill is still sitting in committee without action. If it dies, the people better off will be the sitting Supreme Court justices, who keep lifetime seats, and the political leaders of both parties, who keep a Court shaped by past appointments rather than by recent elections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sitting justices keep lifetime seats so far

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court term-limits bill on May 21, 2025.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred to his committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 86 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, while a Republican-led Judiciary Committee has taken no action since the referral.

industries.note: The nine current justices would lose the effective lifetime tenure the Constitution otherwise provides, being retired one at a time as new justices arrive. Their interest in keeping 30-to-40-year seats runs against a public interest in a Court that regularly refreshes.

industries.industry: Political leaders invested in the current Court's makeup
industries.note: A fixed two-year schedule removes both the jackpot of a surprise vacancy that lets a president lock in decades of influence and the ability to freeze a seat by delaying a nomination. Leaders of both parties lose that leverage; the public gains predictability.

Retired justices could be randomly recalled to fill temporary vacancies while remaining retired from regular service, giving former justices a route back onto the bench. It is a niche benefit to a small group rather than an industry gain.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican chair controlling the House Judiciary Committee's calendar, no Republican cosponsor, and no movement since May, the bill is likely to sit without a hearing for the rest of the Congress, as prior Supreme Court term-limit proposals have. A realistic path to a vote would require Democrats to win the House majority in the 2026 midterm elections.
